about: MP6 and MP8: where a body's elements are, and what its ore deposits hold, as blocks (matter pack design section 5, steps 3 to 6). The composition chain runs each once per element; the sums are also in sse_atoms::matter, held together by a test.

references: McDonough, W. F. and Sun, S.-s. 1995, Chemical Geology 120, 223: the composition of the Earth (CI chondrite and pyrolite). doi:10.1016/0009-2541(94)00140-4
Palme, H. and O'Neill, H. St. C. 2014, Treatise on Geochemistry (2nd ed.) 3, 1: cosmochemical estimates of mantle composition (CI H and O). doi:10.1016/B978-0-08-095975-7.00201-1
Lodders, K. 2003, ApJ 591, 1220: solar system abundances and condensation temperatures of the elements (host phases, table 8). doi:10.1086/375492
atoms.shown: share = ci · ratio / W;  bound O = ci · ratio · o / W;  W = Σ ci · ratio · (1 + o)

equation.name: An element's share of the material it rode in on
equation.formula:
w = ci * r
s = if W <= 0 then 0 else w / W
b = if W <= 0 then 0 else w * o / W

ci.name: its share of CI chondrites by mass

r.name: how much more of it the star has than the Sun

o.name: oxygen its oxide binds, per kg of it

W.name: the same weight summed over the material

b.name: share of the material that is oxygen bound to it

source.text: McDonough, W. F. and Sun, S.-s. 1995, Chemical Geology 120, 223

explain.curious: Every rock and every grain of metal that built a planet carried a little of every element. Gold and platinum rode in with the iron; potassium, uranium and thorium came with the rock. How much a world holds of each follows from how much of its material it collected.
explain.science: An element's mass share of the formation material it condenses with (its host phase, Lodders 2003): its CI chondrite share times its star's abundance over the Sun's, over the same weight summed over every element riding in that material, the oxygen their oxides bind included. Trace elements are shares inside the material, so adding one changes no bulk mass.

params.description: energy per kg that melts chondritic rock, J/kg (the same as the Al-26 block's e_dry)

references: Elkins-Tanton, L. T. 2012, Annual Review of Earth and Planetary Sciences 40, 113: magma oceans in the inner solar system (accretion and Al-26 energy against the energy to melt). doi:10.1146/annurev-earth-042711-105503
atoms.shown: s = min(1, (0.6 · G · M / R + E_Al26) / e_melt)

equation.name: How far a world melted and sorted itself
equation.formula:
heat = 3/5 * G * M / R + max(E, 0)
s = clamp(heat / em, 0, 1)

E.name: aluminium-26 heat left after it formed, per kg

em.name: heat per kg that melts rock

s.name: how far it separated into metal and rock

source.text: Elkins-Tanton, L. T. 2012, Annual Review of Earth and Planetary Sciences 40, 113

explain.curious: A world sorts itself into a metal core and a rocky mantle only if it gets hot enough to melt. Big planets melt from the energy of their own building; small early asteroids melted from radioactive aluminium; small late ones never did, and still hold their metal mixed through their rock.
explain.science: Heat available per kilogram, three fifths of GM/R from accretion plus the Al-26 energy left after the body formed, over the energy to melt chondritic rock. Capped at 1: a world that could melt more than once over separates fully. A process strength, not a class.

references: McDonough, W. F. 2003, Treatise on Geochemistry 2, 547: compositional model for the Earth's core (table 4). doi:10.1016/B0-08-043751-6/02015-6
McDonough, W. F. and Sun, S.-s. 1995, Chemical Geology 120, 223: the composition of the Earth (CI chondrite and pyrolite). doi:10.1016/0009-2541(94)00140-4
atoms.shown: core = s · f · D / (f · D + 1 − f)

equation.name: How much of an element sank with the iron
equation.formula:
fm = clamp(f, 0, 1)
c = if D <= 0 or fm <= 0 then 0 else clamp(s, 0, 1) * fm * D / (fm * D + 1 - fm)

D.name: how much it prefers metal to rock

c.name: share of it in the core

source.text: McDonough, W. F. 2003, Treatise on Geochemistry 2, 547

explain.curious: Iron-loving elements sank with the iron. Nearly all of a planet's gold and platinum is in its core, far out of reach; what is mined at the surface came later, or was brought back up.
explain.science: Mass balance between metal and silicate: with the body's metal share f and the element's partition D (concentration in Earth's core over its silicate, McDonough 2003 and McDonough and Sun 1995), the core holds f·D / (f·D + 1 − f) of it, times how far the world separated. D is one typical value per element, not a function of pressure and oxygen (fudge register).

references: Rudnick, R. L. and Gao, S. 2003, Treatise on Geochemistry 3, 1: composition of the continental crust. doi:10.1016/B0-08-043751-6/03016-4
McDonough, W. F. and Sun, S.-s. 1995, Chemical Geology 120, 223: the composition of the Earth (CI chondrite and pyrolite). doi:10.1016/0009-2541(94)00140-4
atoms.shown: crust = s · fc · E / (fc · E + 1 − fc)

equation.name: How much of the rock's element rose into the crust
equation.formula:
x = clamp(fc, 0, 1)
cr = if E <= 0 or x <= 0 then 0 else clamp(s, 0, 1) * x * E / (x * E + 1 - x)

E.name: how much richer the crust is in it than the mantle

fc.name: the crust's share of the rock

cr.name: share of the rock's element in the crust

source.text: Rudnick, R. L. and Gao, S. 2003, Treatise on Geochemistry 3, 1

explain.curious: When mantle rock partly melts, the elements that do not fit in its crystals go with the melt and rise. So a thin crust holds a large share of a world's potassium, uranium and thorium, and of many metals people mine.
explain.science: Mass balance between crust (share fc of the silicate) and mantle with the element's enrichment E (concentration in Earth's continental crust, Rudnick and Gao 2003, over its primitive mantle, McDonough and Sun 1995): the crust holds fc·E / (fc·E + 1 − fc) of the silicate's element, times how far the world separated. One typical value per element (fudge register).

params.description: mean crust thickness, m (Earth's area-weighted mean is about 17 km, the Moon's about 35 km, Mars's about 50 km)

references: Rudnick, R. L. and Gao, S. 2003, Treatise on Geochemistry 3, 1: composition of the continental crust. doi:10.1016/B0-08-043751-6/03016-4

equation.name: The crust's share of a world's rock
equation.formula:
hh = clamp(h, 0, R)
ri = R - hh
shell = 4/3 * pi * (R * R * R - ri * ri * ri)
fc = clamp(shell * rho / Ms, 0, 1/2)

fc.name: the crust's share of the rock

source.text: Rudnick, R. L. and Gao, S. 2003, Treatise on Geochemistry 3, 1

explain.curious: A planet's crust is a skin: on Earth about half a per cent of the rock by mass. That thin skin is where every mine is.
explain.science: A shell of the given thickness and density at the surface, over the silicate's mass. The thickness is one value until the surface stage hands each world its own (fudge register).

params.description: how many times its star's metal share a Jupiter-mass giant holds (Thorngren et al. 2016: 9.7 plus or minus 1.3)
how fast the share falls with mass (Thorngren et al. 2016: 0.45 plus or minus 0.09)

references: Thorngren, D. P., Fortney, J. J., Murray-Clay, R. A. and Lopez, E. D. 2016, ApJ 831, 64: the mass-metallicity relation for giant planets (Z_planet / Z_star = 9.7 (M / M_Jup)^-0.45). doi:10.3847/0004-637X/831/1/64
atoms.shown: Z_planet = Z_star · a · (M_Jup / M)^b, at most 1

equation.name: How much of a giant is not hydrogen and helium

Zs.name: its star's share of heavy elements by mass

a.name: metal enrichment of a Jupiter-mass giant

b.name: how fast it falls with mass

zp.name: the giant's share of heavy elements by mass

source.text: Thorngren, D. P. et al. 2016, ApJ 831, 64
source.where: the mass-metallicity relation, from 47 warm giants' masses and radii

explain.curious: A gas giant is mostly hydrogen and helium, but not all: rock and ice sank into it as it grew. The smaller the giant, the bigger that share, so Neptune is mostly not gas at all while Jupiter is mostly gas.
explain.science: The heavy-element share of measured warm giants, fitted against mass: Z_planet over Z_star falls as mass to the minus 0.45. The rest is the envelope's hydrogen and helium at the birth cloud's shares. The fit is for giants from about 0.03 to 10 Jupiter masses (fudge register outside it).

params.description: depth the ore is counted to, m: an SSE4 choice; Kesler and Wilkinson 2008's 1.7e11 t is for all depths, so counting it within 3.3 km overstates ore near the surface (fudge F55)
share of a footprint's crust to that depth that is ore: calibrated so that Earth's arcs hold Kesler and Wilkinson's porphyry copper, one value for every kind (fudge register)

references: Kesler, S. E. and Wilkinson, B. H. 2008, Geology 36, 255: Earth's copper resources estimated from tectonic diffusion of porphyry copper deposits (about 1.7e11 t of copper in porphyry deposits at all crustal depths; 3e11 t for all deposit types). doi:10.1130/G24317A.1
Rudnick, R. L. and Gao, S. 2003, Treatise on Geochemistry 3, 1: composition of the continental crust. doi:10.1016/B0-08-043751-6/03016-4
atoms.shown: grade = min(1, c · k);  m = A · h · ρ · f · grade

equation.name: What an ore deposit holds
equation.formula:
g = clamp(c * k, 0, 1)
m = max(A, 0) * h * rho * clamp(f, 0, 1) * g

A.name: area of the deposit or province

c.name: the element's share of the world's crust

k.name: how many times the ore process raised it over the crust

h.name: depth the ore is counted to

f.name: share of that crust that is ore

m.name: mass of the element in the ore

g.name: the element's share of the ore

source.text: Kesler, S. E. and Wilkinson, B. H. 2008, Geology 36, 255
source.where: copper in porphyry deposits at all crustal depths

explain.curious: A mine is a place where something in the rock did the hard work first: hot fluids over a sinking plate, a giant impact's melt pool, a collision squeezing water through a mountain belt. Each gathered a metal from a vast volume of crust into a small one, hundreds or thousands of times richer. How much ore there is comes from where those processes ran.
explain.science: The ore under a footprint is a share of the crust to a depth; its grade is the crust's concentration of the element times the enrichment its process reaches (typical ore grade over the continental crust, Rudnick and Gao 2003). The ore share is one value, calibrated on Earth's porphyry copper; the deposits are part of the crust, never more than it holds.
